passages.happening:
‘This is what the Lord GOD showed me: I saw a basket of summer fruit’ (verse 1). The LORD asks Amos what he sees, and he answers, a basket of summer fruit. ‘The end has come for My people Israel; I will no longer spare them’ (verse 2).

On that day the songs of the temple will turn to wailing, and there will be many dead, lying in silence everywhere (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The fourth vision turns on a play on words. Summer fruit is qayits; the end is qets. The two words sounded almost the same, so a basket of ripe fruit becomes a sign that Israel is ripe for its end. It follows the same question and answer as the plumb line: God asks what Amos sees, Amos answers, and God explains.

The setting is still the wealthy reign of Jeroboam II, when trade flourished and wealth gathered in the hands of a few. The temple songs of verse 3 may be the songs of the shrine at Bethel. The judgment came through Assyria within a generation, ending in the fall of Samaria in 722 BC. These notes name the dead of verse 3 and do not dwell on them.
passages.later: Jeremiah was shown his own vision through a play on words, an almond branch and God watching over his word (Jeremiah 1:11-12). Ezekiel heard the same verdict: ‘The end has come upon the four corners of the land’ (Ezekiel 7:2).
passages.asks: A basket of ripe fruit looked like plenty, and it meant the end. Ask what in your life looks like abundance but may be ripe for a fall. And ask whether you are listening while God still speaks.

passages.t: Merchants who cannot wait for the Sabbath to end
passages.happening: ‘Hear this, you who trample the needy, who do away with the poor of the land’ (verse 4). They ask when the New Moon will be over so they can sell grain, and when the Sabbath will end so they can market wheat. They plan to make the measure small and the price heavy and to cheat with dishonest scales (verse 5). They plan to buy the poor for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, and to sell even the sweepings of the wheat (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
Amos lets the merchants condemn themselves by quoting their own impatient thoughts. Israel's calendar set aside the New Moon, the first day of each month, and the weekly Sabbath as days of rest from ordinary work, trade included. The merchants keep these days outwardly but can hardly wait for them to end.

Their cheating is double. They reduce the ephah, using an undersized basket so the buyer gets less grain, and increase the shekel, using heavy weights so the buyer pays more silver. Money was weighed, not coined, so crooked weights were a standard way to cheat. The law forbade both.

To buy the poor with silver and the needy for sandals probably means debt slavery: a poor family that could not repay even a small debt lost its members into servitude. Selling the chaff with the wheat means passing off the sweepings of the threshing floor as grain.
passages.later: The law said, ‘You shall maintain honest scales and weights’ (Leviticus 19:36). Nehemiah later shut Jerusalem's gates against those who traded on the Sabbath (Nehemiah 13:15-22).
passages.asks: The merchants kept the Sabbath with their bodies and broke it in their hearts. Ask whether your rest is real, or only waiting for work to begin again. And ask whether anything in the way you earn or spend takes from someone who cannot fight back.

passages.t: Darkness at noon, and a famine of the word
passages.happening:
The LORD has sworn by the Pride of Jacob that he will never forget any of their deeds (verse 7). The land will quake and rise and fall like the Nile (verse 8). On that day God will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in daylight (verse 9). He will turn their feasts into mourning and their songs into laments. It will be like mourning for an only son, a bitter day to the end (verse 10).

‘Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord GOD, when I will send a famine on the land’ (verse 11), not of bread or water, ‘but a famine of hearing the words of the LORD’ (verse 11). People will stagger from sea to sea and roam from north to east looking for the word of the LORD, and they will not find it (verse 12). Young women and young men will faint from thirst (verse 13). Those who swear by the gods of Samaria, Dan and Beersheba will fall, never to rise again (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
God's oath by the Pride of Jacob is ironic. It could mean he swears by himself, the one who should be Jacob's pride, or by Jacob's arrogance, which is as fixed as an oath. The rest of the chapter is a string of sayings about that day: earthquake, flood, eclipse, mourning and famine.

Some interpreters connect the sun going down at noon with a total eclipse of the sun visible in the region in 763 BC and recorded in the Assyrian lists that name each year after an official. It would have happened in Amos's lifetime. The text does not say so, and darkness is a common picture for the Day of the LORD, so the link is possible but not certain.

Sackcloth and shaved heads were the standard signs of grief, and mourning for an only son was the deepest grief a family knew, since it meant the end of its name. Dan, in the far north, held Jeroboam I's second golden calf. Beersheba, in the far south of Judah, was an old pilgrim site. The worst famine is the last: a people who silenced God's prophets will look for his word and not find it.
passages.later: Jeroboam I set the second calf at Dan (1 Kings 12:29-30). After years of turning away, Saul sought a word from the LORD and received none (1 Samuel 28:6).
passages.hard:
Would God really keep his word from people who are seeking it?

Verse 12 says people will seek the word of the LORD and not find it, which can sound as if God turns away sincere seekers. Read in its setting, the people who search are those who rejected the prophets when the word was plainly given, and who look for it only when disaster strikes, as Saul sought a word from God after years of disobedience. Many interpreters read the famine as the result of a long refusal: those who silence God's messengers in the end find no messenger left. Others add that the seeking in verse 12 is frantic, not repentant, a search for rescue rather than for God.

The passage stands beside many promises that those who seek God with all their heart will find him (Jeremiah 29:13). It warns against assuming that God's word will always be there to pick up later. It does not tell anyone who is seeking God now that they are shut out.
passages.asks: The worst famine Amos names is a famine of God's word. Ask whether you have treated God's word as something that will always be there when you get round to it. And if you are seeking God now, ask what it would mean to seek him with your whole heart.
